unlisted_practices: Clinicians should not use vibe coding alone to create high-stakes regulated medical devices or any function where failure could lead to patient harm without appropriate technical knowledge or input.
Clinicians who vibe code tools beyond personal prototypes should notify and engage IT and information governance teams, especially where the tool interfaces with hospital networks or infrastructure.

Developers of vibe-coded tools should document prompts, code comments, and version control, using full software development lifecycle documentation and a software bill of materials for patient-facing or clinical decision support tools.
Safeguards on vibe-coded tools should be scaled up when a tool's scope or user base expands to a higher risk tier.
Clinician developers should obtain professional software developer input for patient-facing or clinical decision support tools.

Developers should document the LLM, version, and prompts used, run license-compliance or software composition scans on AI-generated code, rewrite code of unclear provenance, and maintain a software bill of materials to address intellectual property risk.
Clinician developers should build foundational AI literacy, including awareness that LLMs are probabilistic and can hallucinate code, to avoid overreliance.
Clinician developers should test vibe-coded tools for correctness and edge cases and manually review code and outputs before use.
Clinician developers should add features through small, specific, incremental prompts rather than broad commands to keep development controlled and stable.
Clinician developers should use sandboxed execution for agentic coding tools because of the risk of unintended autonomous actions.
Clinician developers should use human-in-the-loop checkpoints when using agentic coding workflows.
Clinician-built prototypes that show promise for commercialisation should be handed over in a structured way to professional product engineering.
